verdicts.reason: The quote supports documentation of a dropped trial set, not a record of all rejected design alternatives or post-result amendments. This is a narrow project-process safeguard rather than an auditable account of researchers' full decision path.

item.problem_title: Registrations record the final protocol and not the alternatives that were rejected
item.problem_statement: An emulation makes many defensible decisions: active comparator, washout period, time zero, grace period, how treatment episodes are constructed, censoring rules, follow-up length and outcome definition. Each has more than one reasonable answer, and the set of answers is the researcher's degrees of freedom. Design guidance exists and states that the operational methods remain scenario dependent, so it narrows the set without closing it. Registrations record the specification that was finally run and not the alternatives considered, the order in which decisions were made, or which were revised after the data were inspected. A final protocol snapshot cannot reveal what was never logged, so a reader cannot distinguish a protocol written once from one converged upon, and no later audit can reconstruct it.
item.paper: A Benchmark, Expand, and Calibration (BenchExCal) Trial Emulation Approach for Using Real-World Evidence to Support Indication Expansions: Design and Process for a Planned Empirical Evaluation.
item.evidence: Two mechanisms record what was rejected: any post-result design change requires a documented amendment before execution, and any trial set dropped at the data-check stage has its reason recorded. This covers the discarded alternatives that the entry says vanish. It stops short of the full problem because the record is internal to one project's process, the amendment trail sits alongside a clinicaltrials.gov registration that shows the final protocol, and nothing requires the earlier stage 1 design iterations to be published.

verdicts.reason: The proposed approach supplies decision-specific calibration concepts and explicitly places decision-changing thresholds in context-specific discussion with the decision maker. It does not establish general adequacy criteria or acceptable residual-confounding thresholds, so partial addressing is the appropriate effect.

item.problem_title: Regulators have no thresholds for adequate emulation, acceptable residual confounding or sufficient sensitivity analysis
item.problem_statement: FDA guidance asks sponsors to describe an approach that supports causal inference and names target trial emulation where appropriate. NICE states that some target trials cannot be adequately emulated and that bespoke data collection may then be preferable. EMA and ICH guidance emphasize fit-for-use data, prespecification and transparent non-interventional design. None supplies an acceptance criterion, and a universal numerical cutoff for emulation adequacy, residual confounding or sensitivity-analysis sufficiency would not be technically defensible if one were offered. What is missing is the defensible version: prespecified, decision-specific criteria covering protocol fidelity, identification plausibility, data fitness, diagnostics, quantitative bias analysis and robustness of the decision itself, agreed before the submission rather than argued after it. item.paper: A Benchmark, Expand, and Calibration (BenchExCal) Trial Emulation Approach for Using Real-World Evidence to Support Indication Expansions: Design and Process for a Planned Empirical Evaluation.
item.evidence: The procedure supplies the shape of a regulatory threshold, a gate on binary agreement in stage 1 plus a tipping point at which the stage 2 conclusion would change, and it requires an assessment of power at least equal to the trial and of covariate balance by standardized difference and c-statistic. It supplies no number: the decision-changing threshold is explicitly left to be negotiated with the decision-making organization case by case, so adequacy of emulation and acceptable residual confounding remain undefined.
item.quote: Therefore, decision‐changing thresholds must be defined in conjunction with the relevant decision‐making organization and aligned with the specific context being considered.

verdicts.reason: The quoted passage addresses the already-recognized within-person dependence from repeated participation through grouped bootstrap inference. A binary calendar-period covariate in one applied emulation neither develops flexible calendar-time adjustment nor examines treatment-by-start-time heterogeneity.

item.problem_title: Sequential emulation creates repeated participation and calendar-time confounding that its efficiency gain conceals
item.problem_statement: Sequential emulation exploits repeated eligibility: a new trial is emulated at each decision point, and a person eligible at many points contributes to many of them. The resulting within-person dependence has been addressed: clustering by person, and confidence-interval procedures for survival outcomes compared across the sandwich estimator, nonparametric bootstrap, jackknife and a linearized estimating function bootstrap, which covers better in the small-sample, low-event-rate regime that motivates the design. What has not been addressed is the calendar-time structure. Trials begun at different times occur under different treatment availability, guidelines and background risk, so a pooled estimate assumes an effect common to start times that differ in all three. item.paper: Hepatic real-world outcomes with obeticholic acid in primary biliary cholangitis (HEROES): A trial emulation study design.
item.evidence: Repeated participation is acknowledged as the price of the precision gain, and the correlation it induces is handled by a grouped bootstrap. What remains uncontrolled is the calendar-time side: control indexes accrue at every qualifying visit from 2016 to 2021 while a patient contributes at most one treated index, and calendar time enters the propensity model only as a binary indicator for before or after 2020. With treated follow-up of 9.3 months against 17.5 months for controls, the index-generating process and calendar period are entangled in a way the variance correction does not touch.
item.quote: By allowing patients to contribute multiple indexes to the analytic data set, we increased the precision of estimated treatment effects, which can be crucial in rare disease studies but must address within-subject correlation in the statistical analysis.

verdicts.reason: The paper applies a grouped bootstrap for within-patient correlation in one cohort, but the quote does not establish valid inference for estimated weights, cloning, site clustering, or large-scale sequence expansion. Applying a computationally intensive procedure is not a scalable default-method contribution.

item.problem_title: Variance estimation after cloning and sequence expansion has no scalable, correct default
item.problem_statement: Sequential emulation and cloning expand a dataset by orders of magnitude: a row per eligible decision point per person, multiplied by the strategies each person is initially compatible with. Two dependence structures result, repeated participation and clone-level copies of one history, and naive standard errors ignore both. Person-clustered sandwich inference handles both scalably when the weights are treated as fixed or the estimating-equation conditions hold, and for parametric marginal structural models with inverse probability weighting there are now evaluated alternatives with simulation guidance on coverage against cost. No default handles the harder case: clone-level dependence together with site clustering and the uncertainty from weights estimated by flexible nuisance models, at sequence-expansion scale. item.paper: Hepatic real-world outcomes with obeticholic acid in primary biliary cholangitis (HEROES): A trial emulation study design.
item.evidence: A defensible variance procedure is supplied and used: a nonparametric bootstrap grouped on patients, 1000 replicates, with intervals taken as bootstrap percentiles and p values from the same distribution. It works because the cohort is 4535 controls and 432 treated patients. Nothing here provides the scalable default the entry asks for: there is no analytic variance for the weighted, sequence-expanded estimator, and the same procedure on a cohort orders of magnitude larger, or with cloning as well as sequence expansion, is not addressed.
item.quote: Inference for the HR was conducted using a nonparametric grouped bootstrap with 1000 replicates that addressed the within-patient correlation of outcomes induced by the study design.

verdicts.reason: Prespecifying a 90-day window is better than choosing it after observing outcomes, but an expert-panel choice for one treatment is not a general selection procedure for grace periods or interval widths. The payload also provides no evidence that this choice resolves the time-grid component.

item.problem_title: No outcome-blind procedure selects the time grid or the grace period
item.problem_statement: An emulated protocol has to fix three times that a randomized trial fixes in one act, when eligibility is assessed, when treatment is assigned, and when follow-up begins, and it has to fix the resolution at which time is measured, because routine data arrive as dated records rather than as scheduled visits. Clone-censor-weight and sequential emulation handle the misalignment; neither chooses the grace period or the interval width, and estimates move with both. A coarse interval lets treatment affect an outcome inside the interval before censoring applies; a fine interval produces high-dimensional nuisance models and unstable weights. Selection tools exist and use outcome information: cross-validated variance has been evaluated as a measure of data support for choosing a discretization. item.paper: Hepatic real-world outcomes with obeticholic acid in primary biliary cholangitis (HEROES): A trial emulation study design.
item.evidence: The grace period is chosen outcome-blind and on stated grounds: 90 days after discontinuation, prespecified in the protocol by nine hepatologists from the 24-hour half-life, hepatic recirculation and reduced clearance under obstruction. That is the procedure the entry says is missing, at least for this component. It is not complete: no sensitivity analysis varies the window, the eligibility grid still follows healthcare encounters rather than a defined schedule, and the treated arm is censored on a rule that has no counterpart in the control arm.
item.quote: Patients in the OCA arm were also censored 90 days after the treatment discontinuation date. The 90-day period was prespecified in the protocol by a panel of 9 expert hepatologists

verdicts.reason: The study directly addresses interference by estimating herd effects in a structured, externally benchmarked cluster-trial setting. Its design assumptions and reliance on an external benchmark mean it does not provide a general solution for observational database emulations, so partial addressing is justified.

item.problem_title: Emulation assumes no interference, and cloning individuals can produce joint strategies nobody could implement
item.problem_statement: One person's treatment can change another's outcome through infection, provider behavior, household exposure or a shared resource constraint. Target trial emulation as normally practiced invokes no interference, and under that assumption an individual-level protocol is coherent. Identifying a direct or spillover effect requires more than adding the interference literature alongside it: the emulation has to specify a feasible joint or stochastic treatment policy, the exposure mapping or potential-outcome indexing that defines what each unit is exposed to, and joint support for that exposure. Individual clone-censor rules do not identify those effects, because a set of individually compatible strategies need not correspond to any allocation a cluster could receive. item.paper: Estimating the herd effects of antimicrobial prevention interventions on ventilator-associated pneumonia within ICU populations: a cluster randomized trial emulation using data from Cochrane reviews.
item.evidence: An estimator for interference is supplied and applied: with an external benchmark tier, the effect on non-recipients becomes identifiable, and it is large, an odds ratio of 2.17 (1.56-3.03) for antibiotic decontamination, larger in magnitude than the direct effect of 0.77 (0.55-1.09) it contaminates. What it does not close is the emulation case: the procedure needs three tiers of externally benchmarked trials, and it offers nothing for an observational emulation in a single database, where no benchmark tier exists and cloned individuals still carry an unexamined no-interference assumption.
item.quote: The new finding arising here is that VAP prevention as a direct effect is not evident for either antiseptic- or antibiotic-based decontamination interventions.

verdicts.reason: External benchmark incidence is used here to interrogate SUTVA and interference, not as a negative control, proxy, validation sample, or joint confounding-control workflow. The quote supports that narrower interference exercise and does not bear on integrating the listed tools into target trial emulation.

item.problem_title: Negative controls, proxies and validation data are not integrated into a standard emulation workflow
item.problem_statement: A correctly implemented emulation prevents specific design-induced temporal biases and does not create exchangeability. Active-comparator new-user designs, high-dimensional propensity scores and richer clinical measurement all reduce residual confounding without guaranteeing it. The tools that address what remains, negative control outcomes and exposures, instrumental variables, proximal causal learning and external validation samples, identify under distinct and partly untestable assumptions and sometimes target different estimands. They therefore cannot be mechanically ordered or combined: doing so requires an explicit joint model aligned to one estimand, and no such model is in use, so there is no convention for reporting what each tool contributed or for reconciling them when they disagree. item.paper: Estimating the herd effects of antimicrobial prevention interventions on ventilator-associated pneumonia within ICU populations: a cluster randomized trial emulation using data from Cochrane reviews.
item.evidence: External benchmark data function here as a negative control: the 109 non-decontamination trials supply the incidence that decontamination trial control groups should have shown, and the gap between 23.3 per 100 and a median of 45.9 per 100 is what makes the assumption testable at all. The procedure is stated in general terms, that testing this assumption requires external benchmark incidence for the endpoint. It is not a workflow: it requires a large external literature on the same endpoint, and no analogous benchmark construction is offered for a database emulation.
item.quote: Although the validity of causal inference from an RCCT crucially depends on SUTVA, testing SUTVA requires reference to external benchmark incidence data for the endpoint of interest.

verdicts.reason: The simulation shows that assumption violations can harm coverage, including in larger samples, but it does not identify unsupported treatment histories or provide a policy-specific support diagnostic. Reporting post-weighting standardized mean differences in the applied analyses does not address the registered gap.

item.problem_title: Positivity diagnostics describe weights instead of naming which patient histories are unsupported
item.problem_statement: A deterministic treatment strategy can assign a treatment that clinicians almost never give to patients with certain covariate histories. The standard response is to inspect the weight distribution and truncate the tail. Truncation is bias-variance regularization: it cannot identify an effect where the treatment density is structurally zero, and a marginal weight summary does not say which intervention-relevant histories carry small or zero density. What a reader needs and does not get is a policy-specific support criterion fixed in advance, diagnostics localized by time and by history, the fraction of the target population that fails the criterion, and the estimand that survives once those strata are set aside. Empirically, poor overlap has been shown to defeat adjustment methods that were otherwise well specified, which is the failure a weight histogram is least able to show. Software
item.paper: Evaluating generalizability of oncology trial results to real-world patients using machine learning-based trial emulations.
item.evidence: A semi-synthetic simulation quantifies what positivity failure costs: bias and confidence interval under-coverage that grow with sample size, so a larger database makes the problem worse rather than better. That is more than a weight summary and it is a real contribution. It stops short of the entry: in the actual emulations the only overlap reporting is that standardized mean differences fell below 0.2 after weighting, and no patient history is named as unsupported, so the simulation shows the consequence without locating the region where it occurs.
item.quote: The simulations additionally showed that larger sample sizes in cases 2, 3 and 4 worsened coverage, suggesting that assumption violations are amplified in larger datasets.
